original_message: In April 1994, following the assassination of President Habyarimana, members of the Hutu majority killed an estimated 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsi, over roughly 100 days. The genocide ended when Tutsi-led RPF forces took control of the country.

chain.text:
In April of '94, everything changed. When President Habyarimana died, it was like a switch flipped. For weeks, our neighbors, people we had known our whole lives, turned against us. The Hutu started killing Tutsis, anyone they could get their hands on. They said it was to protect Rwanda, but all I saw was hate, raw and terrifying.

My family, my uncles, so many friends... they were murdered. My father… he was killed just down the road, by men who used to share tea with us.  I hid for weeks, listening to the screams, praying not to be discovered. 

It wasn't about politics or power, it was pure savagery. They wanted our blood, and they took it without hesitation. The world watched, but few did anything. After 100 days of hell, the RPF came and stopped the killing.  They brought order back to a country shattered by hate.

But the scars remain. We rebuilt Rwanda, tried to forget, to move forward. But I can't erase what happened. The ghosts are still here, in every corner, whispering the names of those who were lost. And the men who organized it all? They live among us, pretending nothing happened. 


It's a burden we carry, this memory. We must remember so that history doesn’t repeat itself.  But remembering isn’t enough. Education, understanding, compassion - these are the tools we need to build a future where such horrors are never again possible.

chain.text:
Ah, you speak of April 1994. That month... it ripped open our world like a storm tearing through a village.  When President Habyarimana died, it felt like darkness fell over everything. Neighbors we shared meals with, played games with, they became strangers filled with something cold and terrible.

They said it was about Rwanda, protecting her. But what I saw were eyes burning with hate, hands reaching for knives and machetes. My uncles, my friends, even my father... gone. Taken by men who once laughed with us, shared stories over tea.  I hid, you see? For weeks, listening to the cries of others being taken, praying each night wouldn't be my last.

It wasn't about politics or power, it was the devil himself whispering in their ears. They wanted our blood, and they took it without a second thought. The world watched, but few stepped in. A hundred days of hell, that's what it felt like. Then came the RPF, like a storm clearing the sky.  They brought order back to a broken land, but the wounds remained.

We built anew, tried to forget, move on. But the past clings to us like a shadow. The ghosts of those lost are everywhere, whispering their names in the wind. And the men who orchestrated this horror? They walk among us, pretending nothing happened.

This memory... it's a heavy burden we carry. To remember is vital, so history doesn't repeat itself. But remembering isn't enough. Education, understanding, compassion… these are the tools to build a future where such darkness never returns. This is my hope, this is why I teach. It's the only way forward.

Ah, you speak of April 1994. That month... it tore through our lives like a whirlwind, leaving nothing but rubble and despair. When President Habyarimana died, it felt like a switch flipped. The neighbors we shared laughs with, played games with – they became strangers, eyes cold and hard, gripped by something dark and terrible.

They said it was about Rwanda, protecting her. But what I saw were those same hands that once helped me build my toy house now reaching for machetes and knives. My father, uncles, friends... gone. Vanished like smoke in the wind, taken by men who once shared tea with us, laughed with us.  I remember hiding, week after week, listening to the cries of others being dragged away, each night a prayer whispered that I wouldn't be next.

It wasn't politics or power that drove them. It was something else entirely, a sickness infecting their hearts and minds. The devil himself whispering lies into their ears. They wanted our blood, spilled like water on the ground. The world watched, but few came to help. One hundred days of hell. A nightmare that clung to us all.

Then came the RPF, like a storm clearing the sky, bringing order to the chaos. But the wounds they inflicted... deep and lasting. We rebuilt, tried to forget, move on. But the past lingers, a shadow stretching across our lives. The ghosts of those lost whisper in the wind, their names etched into my soul. And the men who planned this horror? They walk among us now, pretending nothing happened.

Remembering what happened... it's a heavy burden we carry. To forget would be to betray them, to allow darkness to return. But remembering isn't enough. Education, understanding, compassion – these are the weapons we need to fight against hate and build a future where such darkness never returns. This is my hope. This is why I teach. It's the only way forward.

chain.text:
Ah, April 1994...  My friend, you speak of a wound that still bleeds in every Rwandan heart. When Habyarimana died, it was like a dark cloud descended upon our land. The people we knew, those who shared laughter and food with us - they changed. Their eyes turned cold, their smiles vanished. 

The hate… it spread like a wildfire. Those who once helped build my brother’s toy house were now brandishing machetes, fueled by something monstrous. My father, uncles, friends... they disappeared. Gone in the blink of an eye, taken by men who had shared our teacups and jokes just days before. 

I remember hiding for weeks, listening to the screams echo through the night. Each day felt like a gamble, hoping I wouldn't be next. They said it was about protecting Rwanda, but it wasn't about our country. It was something else entirely, a sickness that took hold of their souls, whispering lies and turning neighbor against neighbor. 

The world watched, but few came to help. A hundred days of pure terror. It felt like the devil himself had come to Earth. Then, like a storm clearing the skies, the RPF arrived, bringing order to the chaos. But the scars they left… deep, lasting wounds that still ache. We rebuilt, tried to forget, but the past lingers. The ghosts of those lost whisper in my ear, their names forever etched upon my soul.

And those who planned this horror? They walk among us now, pretending nothing happened. Remembering what occurred is a heavy burden we carry. To forget would be to betray them, to allow darkness to consume us again. But remembering isn't enough. We need education, understanding, and compassion – these are our weapons against hate. This is my hope, the reason I teach. It’s the only way forward, the only way to ensure that such darkness never returns to our land.
